title: Hazel's Architecture Around #2651
question: How is Hazel built around hazelgrove/hazel#2651 (Statics: a module binding analyzes its definition once, not twice), and what does the PR change in that architecture? From Matthew Hammer and Alexander Bandukwala (Modules II's owner) reviewing #2651 together on 2026-10-21, aiming to merge it that day; Matthew had tested its behaviour and asked how Hazel is built around it.
nothing_timed: Nothing was timed for this report. Six module programs were run and analyzed with the command-line tool built at dev 962a7cb009 and at #2651's 29c08fd8fa ('runs' below); every count is counted from the code; the timings quoted are #2651's own (its description) and hazelgrove/hazel#2609's finding 7.

#2651 commit pushed during the review: code and test comments only
#2651 head since the review: one test's name

method: Six read-only readers of the code at the commits above, one subsystem each (the edit-to-statics pipeline, the statics core, modules, elaboration to evaluation, the PR itself, its performance context); questions for Alexander drafted from two lenses and each checked for its premise and its need; a fact-check of every file:line at the commit its link names (gen024.py checks each linked range exists and writes its first line to drivers/refs-check.txt); figures rendered to PNG with ffmpeg's SVG reader in light and dark colours and looked at; not opened in a browser. Alexander's answers from the review and in conversation were relayed by Matthew and are paraphrased; his later answers on #2651 are paraphrased with a link to each comment. Afterwards the command-line tool was built at dev 962a7cb009 and at 29c08fd8fa and six module programs were run and analyzed with it ('runs'). GitHub (the PR's comments, reviews and checks) last read 2026-10-21 19:34Z. The page was first generated by drivers/gen024.py and has been edited directly since, as the review went on.

questions.question: Alexander, on dev should `module M : { let x : Int } = 5 in M.x` keep evaluating to 5? If so, #2651 must not read back the bare analysis whenever statics lifted the definition into a one-member signature: either it skips the read-back there, or autolabel_singleton_tuple first records what it returns. Either way it gives up the new result that its evaluator test pins for `module M : { let x : Int } = { let x = 1; let y = 2 } in M.x`.
answer: Answered, Alexander, 2026-10-21: dev's result for the module with an extra member (its unelaborated source) is a bug, which comes from the auto-labelling of one-member tuples; that program should evaluate to 1, or be stuck. So #2651's 1 is a correct result: the behaviour change fixes a dev bug, and the PR's test pins the fix.

Answered further, Alexander, on #2651, 2026-10-21. On the evaluator test (his comment): fine; the result matches how labeled tuples work. One could argue for making incompatible signatures stuck, but much of Hazel does not work that way, and his signature-sealing PR would make y private. On the bare value (his comment, answering Matthew's): option 2, accept it. A bare value under a module signature should be stuck and a static error; Modules II part 1 already gives both, with or without #2651, so on dev the missing error is temporary and #2651 needs no special case. Matthew's decision: the test for this program goes on part 1, not in #2651 (his reply).

questions.question: Alexander, can #2651 merge into dev ahead of your Modules II stack, with the one-line conflict in parts 2 to 9 resolved by keeping its read-back and adding `~coercible=true` to its fallback? That resolution is right only if, on your branches, the let's recorded analysis of the definition is the same analysis as the direct pass it replaces.
answer: Answered, Alexander, 2026-10-21, in conversation, relayed by Matthew: he sees no conflict between #2651 and Modules II. He had not yet looked at #2603.

questions.question: Alexander, are module bindings meant never to be recursive, items inside `{ ... }` included, and if so, would you rather the module expansion tell the let that it is not recursive than have ModuleExp spot self-reference from the fixpoint in the let's elaboration, as #2651 now does?
answer: Answered for now, Alexander, 2026-10-21: whether modules should be recursive is not settled. For now it is fine for them not to be recursive by default, since recursion has a number of known correctness problems; whether they should be is a question for Cyrus. On the signal: Modules II has none for this, and he did not write the original module keyword; as things stand a module binding is a let that is not recursive. His suggestion is an argument on the let analysis saying whether to check the recursive case, so that a module binding is never analyzed recursively.

Answered further, Alexander, 2026-10-21. On the module keyword (in conversation, relayed by Matthew; his own agent's reading, which matches ours): it makes the binding non-recursive and allows a capitalized name, and is otherwise a let; #2651 keeps both. On #2651 he asked whether defining a module to be a function should be an error, addressing @disconcision on the self-naming test (his comment; For Cyrus). And on the self-naming signal (his comment): names_itself also matches a fixpoint the user wrote, module m = fix f -> …, which then keeps dev's results but loses the speed-up, and the two cannot easily be told apart by shape; so the signal belongs in the let analysis, as an argument that makes a module binding non-recursive, which can be a follow-up to keep #2651 small, and names_itself could go altogether if binding a module to a function becomes a static error (the guard). Matthew agreed, and a prototype is in progress (his reply).

questions.question: Alexander, on your stack does ModuleExp still need its separate analysis and elaboration of the definition (def_elab_direct, which moduleexp_elab swaps in for the let's), or could a module binding use the let's elaboration as is, as your docs/modules.md already says it does?
answer: Answered, Alexander, 2026-10-21, in conversation, relayed by Matthew, to the question as first asked (is the definition's elaboration before the let wraps it exactly what moduleexp_elab is meant to take?): yes, as he understands it, and it comes from the old elaborator. Reading the definition back from the stored info is closer to the original design than dev's second pass, because the old elaborator also read the definition from the statics map.

questions.question: Alexander, which of these module behaviours do you want pinned as tests in #2651 (a module binding analyzes its definition once): the self-naming error at its exact place, a function-valued module that does not name itself, and a module bound to a bare value under a one-member signature?
answer: Answered on #2651, 2026-10-21. The third, the bare value: Alexander offered to pin it as stuck here, with a note that the static error comes with Modules II part 1, or to leave it out of #2651 and add it on part 1, where it can assert both the stuck term and the error (his comment); Matthew chose part 1 (his reply). The first, the self-naming error: the let-analysis prototype pins the test to its mark, and its tests are to include Alexander's two fix programs (Matthew's reply).

for_cyrus.question: Should module bindings be recursive?
for_cyrus.context: Today module F = … as an expression is not (a self-reference is an error, and #2651 keeps it one), while a module F = … item inside { … } is lowered to a plain let and, by our reading, is. Alexander: for now it is fine for modules not to be recursive by default, since recursion has a number of known correctness problems (question 3).

for_cyrus.question: Should binding a module to something that is not a module be a static error?
for_cyrus.context: module F = fun x -> 1 in F(3) is accepted today. With a signature the case is settled: module M : { let x : Int } = 5 in M.x, accepted on dev, is already a static error, and stuck, on Modules II part 1, which Alexander accepted as the intended behaviour, dev's missing error being temporary (question 1). If a module bound to a function becomes an error too, neither a self-naming function nor a module … = fix … can reach #2651's guard, and names_itself could go (the guard). Alexander asked a form of this on #2651 on 2026-10-21 at 18:25Z, in a review comment on its self-naming test (Test_Statics_Modules.re:411): "should this be an error defining a module to be a function?" (his comment). He addressed it to @disconcision, Andrew Blinn, who wrote the module keyword (b0735de6d6 to 131f508825 are by disconcision, the account Andrew opened #2469 (Modular editors) from), so it can be answered there, by Andrew or Cyrus.

for_cyrus.question: What should the module keyword add over let?
for_cyrus.context: Alexander had favoured plain let for module definitions; Cyrus wanted the keyword to do more. Today a module binding is checked as a let that is not recursive (Modules). By Alexander's reading (his agent's, in conversation, relayed by Matthew), which matches ours, the keyword makes the binding non-recursive and allows a capitalized name, and is otherwise a let; #2651 keeps both.
